newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic expected to prevail in postwar vote.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic expected to prevail in postwar vote.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic appears poised to lead his leftist coalition to victory in weekend federal elections in rump Yugoslavia, his first electoral test since the end of the Yugoslav conflict.
Despite presiding over a devastating war and economic collapse, Milosevic was heading into Sunday's elections in a strong position, according to analysts and opinion polls.
Dropping the nationalist rhetoric that helped lead to old Yugoslavia's violent disintegration, Milosevic has presented himself as the guarantor of peace and stability.

Belgrade commentators said voters in Serbia and Montenegro -- all that is left of the old Yugoslav federation -- like strong leaders and are heavily influenced by state television, which is under strict government control.
"People here are really afraid of any kind of change," Petar Lukovic, an independent political analyst, told Reuters.
Milosevic's coalition and opposition parties held final rallies on Thursday before a 48-hour blackout on campaigning.
The opposition rally in Belgrade's Republic Square drew at least 10,000 people but government television ignored the event.
The state media has shut out the opposition and devoted slavish attention to campaign promotions by the pro-government coalition of Socialists, the Yugoslav United Left and New Democracy party.
Milosevic, who now rarely appears in public, spoke at the coalition's final rally in front of a huge television screen.
"The united forces for peace and development... will celebrate a historical victory over hatred, violence and conservativism," he told supporters in a convention hall.
A state media campaign now blames the tragic war on nationalist paramilitaries, associating them with "Chetniks" who clashed with anti-Nazi partisans during World War Two.
Across town, young rock bands performed at the opposition rally and opposition leaders took the stage to castigate Milosevic's nine-year rule.
The "Together" opposition coalition, which covers the political spectrum from liberal to hardline nationalist, has tried to exploit widespread discontent over plunging living standards.
Opposition leaders for the first time managed to put aside their differences and run on a united list for the federal elections.
But analysts say the opposition lacks a clear, coherent message and seemed not to be reaching a large portion of the public which is dissatisfied but undecided.

With Milosevic's term as Serbian president due to expire next year, diplomats say he wants to win a big majority in the federal parliament so he can amend the constitution and bolster the symbolic office of the federal president.
Voters on Sunday will be choosing municipal authorities and a federal parliament with a 138-member chamber of citizens and a 40-member upper chamber of republics.
Polls for the republican parliament of Montenegro will also be held on Sunday.
